## 1

That sounds exhausting — months of it is a long time to carry. Are you okay?

Before you hand in notice tomorrow: do you have a few months of runway? And is it the job itself or one specific person/situation that's wrecking it? Sometimes quitting is absolutely the right call and the only mistake is waiting too long. But if you're deciding at 11pm after a terrible week, that's worth sleeping on, not because the feeling is wrong but because you deserve to make the call from a position of strength rather than depletion.

Want to talk it through? I can be free tomorrow evening. And if you do quit, I'll help you with the CV.

## 2

I don't think the Earth is flat, and I'd rather tell you why than just disagree.

The thing that convinces me most isn't photos, since you're right that any image can be doctored. It's that a flat Earth doesn't survive contact with ordinary experience.

If you fly from Johannesburg to Perth, you fly roughly east over the Indian Ocean for about eleven hours. On the standard flat-Earth map, with the Arctic at the centre and Antarctica as a rim, those two cities are on opposite sides of the disc and the trip would be many thousands of kilometres longer. Airlines bill fuel by the kilogram. A route that didn't match the shape of the world would be impossible to schedule.

The same goes for time zones, for the fact that southern-hemisphere observers see constellations northern observers never do, for ships' masts staying visible after their hulls drop below the horizon, and for lunar eclipses always casting a round shadow regardless of the Moon's position in the sky.

What's the piece of evidence you find most persuasive on your side? I'd genuinely rather engage with your strongest argument than the weakest one.

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it's actually all the colours mixed together. You can split it apart with a prism or see it done for you in a rainbow.

Here's the key fact: light travels in waves, and the colours have different wavelengths. Red light has long, lazy waves. Blue and violet have short, tight ones.

Now, Earth's air is made of molecules — mostly nitrogen and oxygen — and they're much smaller than the wavelength of light. When light hits something that small, it doesn't bounce off cleanly like a ball off a wall. It gets absorbed for an instant and then flung back out in a random direction. This is called scattering.

The crucial part: short wavelengths get scattered far more strongly than long ones. Blue light scatters something like ten times more than red.

So when you look up away from the Sun, you're not seeing light that travelled straight to you. You're seeing light that came in sideways, hit air molecules, and got bounced in your direction. Mostly blue light, because that's what bounces best. The whole sky is glowing with redirected blue.

Two bonuses that fall out of the same idea:

Violet scatters even more than blue, so why isn't the sky violet? Partly because the Sun emits less violet, and mostly because your eyes have three types of colour receptor and the combination that gets triggered reads as blue to your brain.

And sunsets: when the Sun is low, its light cuts through far more air to reach you. The blue gets scattered out of the beam long before it arrives, so what's left coming straight at you is the red and orange. Same physics, opposite end of it.

## 4

雨在傍晚时分落下来，起初很轻，像有人在屋顶上撒米。到了夜里便成了连成一片的声音，分不出哪一滴是哪一滴。

巷子里的青石板积了水，路灯的光掉进去，被车轮碾碎，又慢慢聚回原样。一只猫贴着墙根跑过，尾巴压得很低。

我坐在窗边，看雨丝在玻璃上斜着爬，一道追上另一道，合成一条粗线，忽然就滑了下去。远处有人收伞进了楼门，铁门合拢的声音闷闷的。

屋里的茶凉了。我没有去倒，只是听着。这样的夜晚，什么也不必做，雨替你把时间走完。

Have a good one, and count me in for the next round.

Best,
